notes.body:
---
title: "A Preacher's Prayer"
author: "Charles Spurgeon"
date: "c. 1875"
topics: [preaching, dependence, the Spirit, weakness]
excerpt: "The most famous preacher of his century, asking not to be listened to."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have the words ready and they are not enough. They were never going to be enough.

Come down on this. Without you I am a man making a noise in a room. Let there be a power here that is not mine, so that nobody goes home admiring the sermon and everybody goes home having met you.

Take me out of the way. If people must remember something, let it be Christ and not the man who spoke about him. And when I have finished, do the work I could not do.

About this prayer: Charles Haddon Spurgeon preached to thousands weekly in London for nearly forty years, and said his whole ministry hung on the Spirit doing what he could not. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Abide in Me"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "1882"
topics: [abiding, union with Christ, dependence, rest]
excerpt: "Murray's central theme: the branch does not strain to stay on the vine."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord Jesus, you did not say "work harder at me". You said abide in me.

I have spent years trying to produce fruit and almost none staying attached. Teach me the difference. A branch does not manufacture grapes by effort; it simply refuses to let go of the vine, and the life does the rest.

Take the whole weight of my keeping onto yourself. I am not able to hold on to you — you must hold on to me. Let me wake tomorrow not resolving to be better, but consenting to be joined.

And where I have made abiding into one more thing to be good at, forgive me, and put me back where I belong: attached, dependent, alive.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray, pastor in the Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa, wrote Abide in Christ in 1882. He wrote over two hundred books, most of them circling this one idea. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Absolute Surrender"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "1895"
topics: [surrender, obedience, the will, consecration]
excerpt: "Murray's hardest book in one prayer — God can only fill what has been emptied."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have been offering you most of myself and calling it everything.

You cannot fill what is already full. So empty me. Take the parts I have kept back on the quiet reasoning that they were small, or mine by right, or too tangled to hand over. Take the ones I do not yet know about.

I am not surrendering because I am strong enough to. I am surrendering because you asked, and because holding on has not worked. Do the surrendering in me — I cannot even give myself away without your help.

And having taken everything, be everything. That is the only trade worth making.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray gave the addresses that became Absolute Surrender at conventions in the 1890s. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Awakening/Give Me a Heart to Praise You.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Give Me a Heart to Praise You"
author: "Charles Wesley"
date: "1742"
topics: [new heart, holiness, love, sincerity]
excerpt: "The hymn-writer asks for the one thing he cannot manufacture."
tags: [prayer]
---
Give me a heart that can praise you — a heart that is humble, thankful, true, where you alone are living, and where you write your new name.

Give me a heart that trusts, that is submissive, meek. Give me the lowly mind that was in Christ. Give me a heart that feels his blood so freely spilled for me — a heart that is soft, and warm, and clean, full of love, full of God.

Take away what I have and give me what you are.

About this prayer: Charles Wesley wrote something like six thousand hymns. This is from "O for a Heart to Praise My God" (1742), reworked here as prose. Rendered in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Awakening/Hold Not Our Sins Up Against Us.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Hold Not Our Sins Up Against Us"
author: "Søren Kierkegaard"
date: "c. 1848"
topics: [forgiveness, mercy, honesty, grace]
excerpt: "Kierkegaard turns the request around: hold up our sins, but hold up your grace higher."
tags: [prayer]
---
Father in heaven, do not hold our sins up against us. Hold us up against our sins — so that the thought of you, when it comes to mind, is not a reminder of what we have done wrong, but of what you have forgiven. Not of how we drifted, but of how you saved us.

You are not a God who is far off and unmoved. You are near, and you are moved.

Teach me that the opposite of sin is not being good. The opposite of sin is faith.

About this prayer: Søren Kierkegaard, the Danish philosopher whose books did more than any others in his century to make Christian faith uncomfortable for comfortable Christians. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Awakening/I Am Not What I Ought to Be.md
notes.body:
---
title: "I Am Not What I Ought to Be"
author: "John Newton"
date: "c. 1790"
topics: [grace, assurance, growth, repentance]
excerpt: "The former slave-trader's honest account of his own progress."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I am not what I ought to be. I am not what I wish to be. I am not even what I hope to be.

But I am not what I once was. And by your grace, I am what I am.

Let that be enough to keep me going and never enough to let me stop. Where I am still the man I was, break it. Where you have changed me, let me not take the credit. Amazing grace it was, and amazing grace it still has to be.

About this prayer: John Newton captained a slave ship before his conversion, later became an Anglican curate, wrote "Amazing Grace", and spent his last years campaigning against the slave trade alongside William Wilberforce. The first two paragraphs are close to his own words. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Lead, Kindly Light"
author: "John Henry Newman"
date: "1833"
topics: [guidance, darkness, one step, trust]
excerpt: "Becalmed on a boat in the Mediterranean, Newman asks only for the next step."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lead, kindly light, through the dark that is around me. Lead me on.

The night is dark and I am a long way from home. Lead me on. Keep my feet. I am not asking to see the far horizon — one step is enough for me.

I was not always like this. I used to choose my own road, and I liked to see a long way ahead. I loved the bright day and, in spite of every fear, my pride ruled me. Do not remember those years.

You have kept me this far. You will keep me still, over moor and marsh, over crag and torrent, until the night is gone.

About this prayer: John Henry Newman wrote it in 1833 while stuck for a week on a becalmed orange boat between Sicily and Marseilles, ill and desperate to get home. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Lord, Give Me China"
author: "Hudson Taylor"
date: "c. 1855"
topics: [mission, calling, faith, provision]
excerpt: "A young man with no money and no committee behind him, asking for a country."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, give me China. Not a career in it — the thing itself, the people, the inland provinces nobody will go to.

I have no money and no society behind me and no obvious qualification. That is not an obstacle to you; it is the arrangement. If the work is yours, you will fund it. If it is not, I would rather find out now.

Do not let me raise support by talking people into it. Let me ask you and tell no one else. And when it comes, let everyone see who sent it.

About this prayer: James Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission on the principle of asking God and never soliciting funds. By his death in 1905 the mission had over eight hundred missionaries. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Lord, Teach Us to Pray"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "c. 1885"
topics: [prayer, teachability, intercession, abiding]
excerpt: "Murray takes the disciples' one recorded request and makes it his own."
tags: [prayer]
---
Blessed Lord, you never taught your disciples how to preach — only how to pray. You knew that a man who can pray will learn the rest, and a man who cannot will be no use however well he speaks.

So teach me. Not techniques. Teach me the thing itself.

Do not let me be satisfied with having prayed. Make me a person who prays. Take me past asking for what I want, into wanting what you want, until the asking and the wanting are the same thing.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray, South African pastor and writer, wrote With Christ in the School of Prayer in 1885. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Make Me Humble"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "1895"
topics: [humility, pride, self-knowledge, grace]
excerpt: "Murray on humility as the one virtue you cannot notice yourself having."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, humility is not thinking less of myself. It is thinking of myself less, and I cannot even manage that by trying.

Every time I catch myself being humble, I have already lost it. So do not give me humility as an achievement. Give it as a by-product of seeing you clearly, the way a man stops discussing his own height when he walks out under the stars.

Let me be genuinely glad when someone else is preferred. Let me hear criticism without immediately assembling the defence. Let me be nothing, and be content to be nothing, because you are everything.

Take the effort out of it. Just show me you, until the question of my own standing quietly stops being interesting.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray's Humility (1895) is the shortest of his books and the one he seems to have most meant. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Make Me Over Again"
author: "George MacDonald"
date: "c. 1880"
topics: [obedience, transformation, childlikeness, will]
excerpt: "MacDonald's insistence that obeying comes before understanding."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have been trying to understand you into obedience, and it has never once worked. Let me obey first and understand afterwards, the way a child does.

I do not ask you to improve me. Improvement leaves the old thing standing. Make me over again.

I am not asking to be spared trouble either. I am asking that whatever comes, it does its work — that it drives me to you rather than away, and that when it is finished I am more yours than I was.

About this prayer: George MacDonald, Scottish minister, novelist and poet, whose Unspoken Sermons C.S. Lewis credited with converting his imagination. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Take My Life"
author: "Frances Ridley Havergal"
date: "1874"
topics: [consecration, surrender, service, offering]
excerpt: "Written in one night after a house full of people came to faith — a life itemised and handed over."
tags: [prayer]
---
Take my life, and let it be set apart for you.

Take my hands and let them move at your impulse. Take my feet and let them be quick and beautiful for you. Take my voice and let me sing always, only, for you. Take my lips and let them be filled with what you want said.

Take my money — every penny of it. Take my mind and use every power as you choose. Take my will and make it yours; it is no longer my own. Take my heart; it is your throne. Take my love; take me.

About this prayer: Frances Ridley Havergal wrote it in February 1874 after every one of the ten people staying in a house with her came to faith over a few days. She later wrote that she had to give away her jewellery to mean the money verse honestly. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "The Covenant Prayer"
author: "John Wesley"
date: "1755"
topics: [surrender, obedience, covenant, new year]
excerpt: "The prayer Methodists have renewed every New Year for two and a half centuries."
tags: [prayer]
---
I am no longer my own, but yours.

Put me to what you want. Rank me with whoever you want. Put me to doing, put me to suffering. Let me be used for you or set aside for you. Let me be lifted high for you or brought low for you. Let me be full, let me be empty. Let me have everything, let me have nothing.

Freely and wholeheartedly, I hand it all over to what you please and what you decide.

And now, glorious and blessed God — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — you are mine and I am yours. Let it be so. And let the covenant I have made on earth be kept in heaven. Amen.

About this prayer: John Wesley introduced a covenant service in 1755, reworking older Puritan forms including Richard Baxter's. Methodists still renew it at the start of each year. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "The Inner Chamber"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "c. 1895"
topics: [prayer, solitude, secret place, discipline]
excerpt: "On shutting the door — the room where nobody can see whether you prayed or not."
tags: [prayer]
---
Father, you told me to go into my room and shut the door, and it is the shutting I keep failing at.

Not the room — I can find a room. It is the door. Everything comes in with me: the list, the phone, the argument I am still having in my head with someone who is not here.

Meet me in there anyway. Let the closed door be a fact rather than a feeling. And let what happens in secret slowly become the truest part of my life, so that the person nobody sees and the person everybody sees are finally the same man.

You who see in secret: that is enough of an audience.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray wrote The Inner Chamber and the Inner Life on the practice of private prayer. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Waiting on God"
author: "Andrew Murray"
date: "1896"
topics: [waiting, patience, silence, trust]
excerpt: "The daily discipline of arriving with nothing to say and staying anyway."
tags: [prayer]
---
My soul, wait only on God.

Not on the answer. Not on the feeling. Not on the sense that something is happening. On God.

Lord, I am so used to measuring prayer by what it produces that a quiet morning feels like a wasted one. Break that in me. Teach me that waiting is not the delay before the real thing — it is the real thing, because it is time spent with you and not with your gifts.

Do your work in the waiting. And when nothing seems to come of it, let me come back tomorrow anyway.

About this prayer: Andrew Murray wrote Waiting on God in 1896 as thirty-one short daily readings, one per month-day. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/A Prayer for Every Hour of the Day.md
notes.body:
---
title: "A Prayer for Every Hour of the Day"
author: "John Chrysostom"
date: "c. 390"
topics: [daily prayer, mercy, guidance, rhythm]
excerpt: "Chrysostom's twenty-four short petitions, one for each hour — a whole day handed over in pieces."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, do not take your mercy away from me. Lord, keep me from thinking anything I should not. Lord, take away all pride and vanity from me. Lord, give me the strength to be patient. Lord, protect me from lying and from speaking carelessly.

Lord, give me an honest thought when I wake, an honest word when I speak, and honest work when I use my hands. Lord, keep me from wanting what is not mine. Lord, teach me to pray, to hope, to believe, to love, to be patient, and to forgive.

Lord, let me not be dragged around by my own appetites. Lord, save me from despair when things go badly and from complacency when they go well. Lord, let me see my own faults and stop weighing up everyone else's.

Lord, whatever this day brings, let it find me thanking you. Into your hands I put my body and my soul. You are the one who made me, and the one who saves me, and the one I belong to. Amen.

About this prayer: John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, wrote a petition for each of the twenty-four hours. It is condensed and rendered here in modern English. The idea is not to say it all at once but to reach for one line at whatever hour you are in.

---
title: "A Prayer for Peace"
author: "Clement of Rome"
date: "c. 96"
topics: [peace, unity, the church, authority]
excerpt: "One of the oldest Christian prayers outside the New Testament — a letter from Rome to a divided church."
tags: [prayer]
---
We ask you, Master, to be our help and our strength. Rescue the ones under pressure, have mercy on the ones who have been brought low, lift up the ones who have fallen. Show yourself to the ones in need, heal the sick, bring back those of your people who have wandered off. Feed the hungry, get your prisoners out, steady the shaky, encourage the discouraged.

Let every nation come to know that you are God alone, that Jesus Christ is your servant, and that we are your people and the sheep of your pasture.

Give harmony and peace to us and to everyone living on the earth, as you gave it to our fathers when they called on you in faith and truth.

About this prayer: Clement, a leader of the church in Rome, sent it to the church in Corinth around AD 96 — while some of the people who had known the apostles were still alive. It is among the earliest Christian prayers we have on paper. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/At the Rising of the Sun.md
notes.body:
---
title: "At the Rising of the Sun"
author: "Hippolytus of Rome"
date: "c. 215"
topics: [morning, work, discipline, daily prayer]
excerpt: "The daily rhythm of a third-century congregation, written down for people who could not read."
tags: [prayer]
---
When you wake, before you touch anything else, wash your hands and pray.

Pray at the third hour, remembering that this was the hour he was nailed to the wood. Pray at the sixth hour, when the day went dark and the whole creation seemed to mourn. Pray at the ninth hour, when water and blood came from his side. Pray before you sleep, and pray again in the middle of the night, when the whole creation is still for a moment and everything praises you.

Lord, let the hours of my ordinary day be pegged to what you did in yours. Let me never get so far into the afternoon that I have forgotten what the afternoon is for.

About this prayer: Hippolytus of Rome set out the daily prayer pattern of the early church in the Apostolic Tradition, around AD 215. The hours he names became the monastic offices. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/Breathe in Me, Holy Spirit.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Breathe in Me, Holy Spirit"
author: "Augustine of Hippo"
date: "c. 400"
topics: [Holy Spirit, guidance, holiness, surrender]
excerpt: "Five short lines asking the Spirit to take over the ordinary machinery of a life."
tags: [prayer]
---
Breathe in me, Holy Spirit, so that my thinking may all be holy.

Act in me, Holy Spirit, so that my work, too, may be holy.

Draw my heart, Holy Spirit, so that I love only what is holy.

Strengthen me, Holy Spirit, so that I defend everything that is holy.

Guard me, then, Holy Spirit, so that I am always holy.

About this prayer: long attributed to Augustine and prayed in his name for centuries. Short enough to hold in your head on a walk, and hard enough to mean it. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Come, Holy Spirit"
author: "Ambrose of Milan"
date: "c. 385"
topics: [Holy Spirit, light, morning, strength]
excerpt: "A morning hymn-prayer from the bishop who baptised Augustine."
tags: [prayer]
---
Come, Holy Spirit, and fill the hearts of the people who belong to you. Light a fire in us — your kind of fire.

You are the one who gathered people out of every language on earth into a single faith. Do it again in us.

Lord, drive back the dark that is in me. Take out of my heart everything that is wrong there, and give me back the light I lost.

About this prayer: Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the late fourth century, wrote hymns for ordinary congregations to sing — partly to teach doctrine to people who could not read. This one has been prayed at the start of Christian gatherings ever since. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "For the Whole Creation"
author: "Basil the Great"
date: "c. 370"
topics: [creation, compassion, animals, stewardship]
excerpt: "Basil widens the circle of prayer to include the animals and the earth itself."
tags: [prayer]
---
God, enlarge in us the sense that we belong to everything alive. Our brothers and sisters are not only the people around us — they are the animals too, the ones you gave the earth to share with us.

We are ashamed of how our race has treated them. We have ruled by force where we were asked to care. We have taken the sound of the earth and turned it into a groan, and the voice that should have risen to you as a song we have made into a cry of pain.

Remember, Lord, that they have loved the sweetness of life just as we do, and served you in their own way better than we have often served you in ours.

About this prayer: Basil of Caesarea, one of the great teachers of the fourth-century church, is widely credited with this. It is one of the oldest prayers in Christian tradition to speak of creation as kin rather than as raw material. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/Give the Spirit Power to Climb.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Give the Spirit Power to Climb"
author: "Boethius"
date: "c. 524"
topics: [light, truth, clarity, seeking God]
excerpt: "Written in a prison cell while awaiting execution — a mind asking to see clearly again."
tags: [prayer]
---
Father, give my spirit the strength to climb to where the clear light is. Let me see the fountain everything good runs from. Give me sight.

Scatter the fog and the weight of this earth from around me, and shine out in your own brightness — because you are the clear sky, you are the quiet resting place for everyone who is faithful.

To see you is where we were going all along. You are the beginning, the vehicle, the guide, the road, and the end.

About this prayer: Boethius, a Roman senator and philosopher, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution around AD 524. This prayer is at the centre of it. The book was read and translated for the next thousand years — by King Alfred, by Chaucer, by Elizabeth I. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/Late Have I Loved You.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Late Have I Loved You"
author: "Augustine of Hippo"
date: "c. 400"
topics: [repentance, beauty, seeking God, conversion]
excerpt: "Augustine's lament over the years he spent looking for God everywhere except where God was."
tags: [prayer]
---
Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new — late have I loved you. And all that time you were inside me, and I was outside, and out there I went looking for you. I threw myself, misshapen as I was, at the beautiful things you had made. You were with me, and I was not with you. Those things held me far away from you — things that would not even exist unless they existed in you.

You called and shouted and broke through my deafness. You blazed and shone and drove away my blindness. You breathed your fragrance over me, and I drew breath, and now I am gasping for you. I tasted you, and now I am hungry and thirsty. You touched me, and I am on fire for your peace.

About this prayer: from Book X of Augustine's Confessions. He is roughly forty-five, looking back on a life that took a long detour. It is the prayer of anyone who came to faith later than they wish they had. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Prayer at the Stake"
author: "Polycarp of Smyrna"
date: "c. 155"
topics: [martyrdom, thanksgiving, courage, trust]
excerpt: "An old bishop thanks God out loud while the fire is being built around him."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord God Almighty, Father of your beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ — I know you through him, and through him I have come to know you.

I bless you for counting me worthy of this day and this hour, worthy to be numbered among your martyrs, and to share the cup of your Christ.

I praise you for everything. I bless you. I give you glory, through the eternal high priest Jesus Christ, your beloved Son. Through him and with him and in the Holy Spirit, glory be to you, now and for ever. Amen.

About this prayer: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostle John, prayed aloud at the stake in about AD 155. He was eighty-six. When the proconsul offered him his life if he would curse Christ, he answered that Christ had never wronged him in all those years. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/Prayer for a Teachable Mind.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Prayer for a Teachable Mind"
author: "Origen of Alexandria"
date: "c. 240"
topics: [scripture, study, humility, the word]
excerpt: "The early church's greatest Bible scholar asking not to be clever at the text."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord Jesus, you opened the Scriptures to the two on the road, and their hearts burned while you spoke. Open them to me.

Do not let me be quick where I should be slow. Do not let me settle a hard passage just to be finished with it. When I find something that overturns what I came in believing, give me the honesty to let it stand rather than filing it down to fit.

You are the Word. Everything written points at you. Keep me from becoming a person who knows the pointing and misses the person.

About this prayer: Origen of Alexandria was the early church's most prodigious biblical scholar, and its most argued-over. Drawn from his homilies on the Scriptures and rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/Prayer Over the Broken Bread.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Prayer Over the Broken Bread"
author: "The Didache"
date: "c. 100"
topics: [communion, unity, the church, thanksgiving]
excerpt: "The oldest Christian communion prayer we have — the scattered grain made one loaf."
tags: [prayer]
---
We thank you, our Father, for the life and the knowledge you made known to us through Jesus your servant. Glory be to you for ever.

As this broken bread was once scattered as grain across the hills, and was gathered and became one loaf, so let your church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom. Yours is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ for ever.

Remember your church, Lord. Save her from all evil and make her complete in your love. Gather her from the four winds, made holy, into the kingdom you have prepared for her.

About this prayer: from the Didache, a short manual of Christian practice written around AD 100 — possibly the earliest Christian document outside the New Testament. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "The Lenten Prayer"
author: "Ephrem the Syrian"
date: "c. 370"
topics: [repentance, humility, self-control, Lent]
excerpt: "The prayer the Eastern church has repeated through every Lent for sixteen centuries."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord and Master of my life, keep away from me the spirit of laziness, of despair, of wanting to run everything, and of talking too much.

Give your servant instead a spirit of purity, of humility, of patience, and of love.

Yes, Lord and King, let me see my own sins and stop condemning the person next to me — because you are blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

About this prayer: Ephrem the Syrian, deacon and hymn-writer, gave the church what is still the central prayer of Lent in the East, said with a full bow at each line. Three requests, one honest confession, and nothing wasted. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "You Beyond All Things"
author: "Gregory of Nazianzus"
date: "c. 380"
topics: [worship, mystery, praise, the Trinity]
excerpt: "A theologian runs out of words and says so — the most honest hymn in the fathers."
tags: [prayer]
---
You beyond everything — what else can I call you? What words can praise you, when no word says you? What mind can take you in, when no mind grasps you?

You alone cannot be spoken, because everything spoken came out of you. You alone cannot be known, because everything known came out of you.

Everything that exists calls to you, and everything that does not yet exist. All things honour you — the ones that can speak, and the ones that cannot. Everything longs for you. Everything that understands anything at all is aiming, without knowing it, at you.

Have mercy, you who are beyond everything. What else can I call you?

About this prayer: Gregory of Nazianzus, archbishop of Constantinople and one of the theologians who settled the church's language about the Trinity, ends by admitting language cannot do it. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Church Fathers/You Have Made Us for Yourself.md
notes.body:
---
title: "You Have Made Us for Yourself"
author: "Augustine of Hippo"
date: "c. 400"
topics: [restlessness, longing, praise, conversion]
excerpt: "Augustine's opening cry in the Confessions — the restless heart that only God can settle."
tags: [prayer]
---
You are great, Lord, and there is no measuring your greatness. Your power has no limit and your wisdom has no end. And here is a man, one small piece of what you made, wanting to praise you — a man carrying his own mortality around with him, carrying the evidence of his own sin and the evidence that you resist the proud. Still he wants to praise you.

You are the one who stirs him to find delight in praising you, because you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

Let me know you, you who know me. Let me know you as fully as I am known. You are the strength of my soul — come into it and make it fit for yourself, so that you can have it and hold it, without stain or wrinkle.

About this prayer: Augustine of Hippo opens his Confessions (Book I) with it around AD 397–400. It has probably done more than any other sentence in Christian history to name what people feel and cannot explain. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "A Prayer for Holy Thirst"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [hunger for God, desire, seeking God, complacency]
excerpt: "An original prayer on the theme of spiritual thirst — that wanting God is itself a gift."
tags: [prayer]
---
God, my worst condition is not that I am far from you. It is that I have got comfortable at this distance.

I have enough religion to be respectable and not enough to be ruined by you. I can go weeks without missing you. That, and not any particular sin, is what frightens me.

So give me back the thirst. Make me want you the way I once wanted things I have since got and grown bored of. If satisfaction at this level is the obstacle, take the satisfaction. I would rather be hungry and awake than full and asleep.

And when the thirst comes, do not let me mistake it for the goal. It is only the road. You are the water.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection, on the theme A.W. Tozer pursued throughout The Pursuit of God (1948) — that spiritual desire is itself God's gift and its absence the real danger. His own words are not reproduced here; the book is short and worth reading whole.

notes.path: Prayers/Modern/A Prayer to Be Satisfied in God.md
notes.body:
---
title: "A Prayer to Be Satisfied in God"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [joy, satisfaction, desire, worship]
excerpt: "An original prayer on the theme that God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him."
tags: [prayer]
---
Father, I keep going to smaller wells. Not evil ones, most of the time — just smaller. A good meal, a good result, a good opinion of me. They work for an hour and then they stop working, and I go back and drink again.

You are not asking me to want less. You are asking me to want you more, because you are the only thing big enough to be wanted the way I am able to want. Make me hungry in the right direction.

Do not let me settle for being useful to you. Let me enjoy you. Let me find that obeying you is not the price of joy but the shape of it. And when the smaller wells run dry — as they will — let that be a mercy that turns me around rather than a loss that just makes me bitter.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection, on the theme John Piper calls Christian hedonism — the conviction that God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him. Piper develops it at length in Desiring God (1986); his own words are not reproduced here.

notes.path: Prayers/Modern/Praying Like a Monk in an Ordinary Week.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Praying Like a Monk in an Ordinary Week"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [rhythm, ordinary life, daily prayer, attention]
excerpt: "An original prayer for someone with no monastery, no silence, and forty minutes of commute."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I do not have a cloister. I have a commute, a phone that will not stop, and a house that gets loud at half past six.

The monks did not have better souls than me. They had better fences. So give me fences — a fixed hour, a fixed page, a fixed place, kept badly but kept. Let me stop waiting for a quiet life before I start a praying one.

Teach me the small hours: something said before my feet hit the floor, something said over the kettle, something said in the car, something said in the dark before sleep. Not because you need the schedule, but because I do.

And when I miss a week, do not let me treat it as evidence. Let me just begin again, today, at this hour, which is the only one I have.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection. The theme is drawn from Tyler Staton's Praying Like Monks, Living Like Fools (Zondervan, 2022) — a book about recovering ancient prayer practice in ordinary modern life. Worth reading in full; none of its text is reproduced here.

---
title: "The Beggar's Prayer"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [prayer, dependence, weakness, asking]
excerpt: "An original prayer on asking — for people who feel they should be past needing to."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have been trying to pray like someone who has his life together, and it has made my prayers thin.

Let me come the way the blind man came, shouting over the crowd telling him to be quiet. Let me come the way the friends came, taking the roof off because the door was blocked. Let me come with nothing but the nerve to ask.

I am not asking you to make me strong enough to stop asking. I am asking you to make me honest enough to keep asking. Prayer is not the report I file after I have managed. It is the line I use because I cannot.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection. The theme — that prayer is the posture of the needy rather than the accomplished — runs through Luke's Gospel and through much of the Reformed devotional tradition. No copyrighted text is reproduced here.

---
title: "The Gaze of the Soul"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [faith, attention, looking to Christ, habit]
excerpt: "An original prayer on faith as a direction of attention rather than a single decision."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I keep treating faith as something I did once, when it is something eyes do continually.

The Israelites in the desert did not have to understand the bronze serpent. They had to look at it. That is all. And the looking had to keep happening, because a man who looks once and then turns away is looking at something else now.

So teach my attention. It drifts to the phone, to the grievance, to the plan. Let it drift back to you a hundred times a day — badly, distractedly, but back.

Let this become a habit rather than a heroism. Not a mountaintop. A direction I keep returning to until it is simply where my eyes rest.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection, on the theme A.W. Tozer calls the gaze of the soul — faith as a sustained direction of attention toward Christ rather than a completed transaction. The chapter is in The Pursuit of God; none of its text appears here.

---
title: "The Veil of Self"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [self, surrender, the cross, hindrance]
excerpt: "An original prayer on the one thing standing between a soul and God."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, the curtain in the temple tore top to bottom and there is nothing left between us — except me.

Self-confidence, self-pity, self-defence, self-display. Not gross sins. Respectable ones, the kind that get a man promoted. They are woven into me so finely that tearing them out will feel like tearing out tissue, because it is tissue. It is mine.

I am not asking you to trim it. Trimming leaves the thing standing. Tear it.

I will flinch. Do it anyway. Whatever it costs, I would rather be torn open to you than left intact and separated.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection, on a theme A.W. Tozer develops in The Pursuit of God — the inner veil of self-life as the last obstacle between a person and God, and the fact that it must be torn rather than tidied. Tozer's text is in copyright and none of it appears here.

---
title: "When Nothing Happens"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [unanswered prayer, perseverance, silence, faith]
excerpt: "An original prayer for the long stretch when God does not seem to be answering."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have asked for this so many times that I am starting to feel foolish asking again.

I do not know whether you are saying no, or not yet, or saying something I am not equipped to hear. I only know the silence is loud, and I am tired.

Keep me from two exits. Do not let me quit and call it maturity. And do not let me manufacture an answer just so the waiting can stop.

Hold me in the middle. Let me keep bringing it to you unfinished. And if the answer, when it comes, is not the one I asked for — let me still be here, and still be yours.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection. Written for the person praying the same thing for the fifth year running.

---
title: "You Are Not Like Anything"
author: "Written for this collection"
date: "2026"
topics: [majesty, worship, transcendence, reverence]
excerpt: "An original prayer against a God cut down to a comfortable size."
tags: [prayer]
---
God, I have made you manageable, and that is a kind of blasphemy that never feels like one.

I compare you to the best things I know and assume you are those things, larger. You are not larger. You are other. Nothing I have met is a scale model of you. Every picture I hold of you is smaller than you and I keep mistaking the picture for the fact.

Correct me. Not by frightening me — by showing me. Let the God I actually pray to be the God who is, and not the one I have quietly assembled out of my preferences and my upbringing.

And when I see even a little of it, teach me what to do next, which is not to explain it. It is to fall silent, and then to worship.

About this prayer: original, written for this collection, on the conviction behind A.W. Tozer's The Knowledge of the Holy (1961) — that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us, and that a diminished picture of God diminishes everything downstream. No text from that book is reproduced here.

---
title: "A Pastor's Prayer"
author: "Aelred of Rievaulx"
date: "c. 1160"
topics: [leadership, weakness, pastoral care, love]
excerpt: "An abbot admits he cannot carry the people in his care, and asks anyway."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, you know I am not equal to this. You know how weak I am, and how little I want to admit it.

You gave me these people. I did not make them and I cannot keep them. Teach me to be, for them, the sort of person I need you to be for me — patient with the slow one, gentle with the frightened one, honest with the one who is fooling himself, and never so busy managing them that I stop loving them.

Sweet Lord, let me not be a hireling among them. Let their burdens be mine and mine be yours, so that I am not crushed by carrying alone what you never asked me to carry alone.

About this prayer: Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx in Yorkshire, wrote his Pastoral Prayer for himself, not for publication. He is the great medieval writer on Christian friendship. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "All Shall Be Well"
author: "Julian of Norwich"
date: "c. 1395"
topics: [hope, suffering, trust, assurance]
excerpt: "The most quoted sentence in English mystical writing, prayed from a sickbed."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, you did not say I would not be battered, or worn out, or shaken. You said I would not be beaten.

Everything is going to be all right. All manner of things are going to be all right.

You are the ground I stand on, and you are what I am asking for, and you are everything.

About this prayer: Julian of Norwich, an anchoress who lived in a cell attached to a church in Norwich, wrote it after a near-fatal illness in 1373 during which she received a series of visions. Hers is the earliest surviving book in English written by a woman. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Be a Bright Flame Before Me.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Be a Bright Flame Before Me"
author: "Attributed to Columba"
date: "c. 590"
topics: [guidance, protection, journeys, shepherding]
excerpt: "Columba of Iona, asking God to go ahead as fire, star and path."
tags: [prayer]
---
Be a bright flame in front of me, God. Be a guiding star above me. Be a smooth path under me, and a kind shepherd behind me — today, tonight, and for ever.

I am tired, and alone, and a stranger here. Steer me toward the harbour of peace.

About this prayer: attributed to Columba, the Irish monk who left Ireland in 563 and founded the monastery on Iona, from which much of Scotland and northern England was evangelised. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Before Study"
author: "Thomas Aquinas"
date: "c. 1270"
topics: [study, wisdom, learning, work]
excerpt: "The prayer Aquinas said before opening a book — for anyone whose work is thinking."
tags: [prayer]
---
Creator beyond describing, you set the order of the universe in place. You are the true source of light and wisdom.

Pour some of your brightness into the dark of my understanding. Take away from me the double darkness I was born into — ignorance and sin.

Make my mind sharp enough to grasp things, my memory strong enough to hold them, my method careful enough to learn well, and my words clear enough to explain it. Show me where to start, guide me while I am in the middle of it, and let me finish. Amen.

About this prayer: Aquinas prayed this before study and teaching. It has been used in universities for seven hundred years, and it still works for anyone who sits down to a hard problem. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Christ With Me — St Patrick's Breastplate.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Christ With Me — St Patrick's Breastplate"
author: "Attributed to Patrick"
date: "c. 800"
topics: [protection, presence, Trinity, morning]
excerpt: "The great encircling prayer of the Irish church — Christ named on every side."
tags: [prayer]
---
I get up today with the strength of heaven behind me: the light of the sun, the brightness of the moon, the flash of fire, the speed of lightning, the swiftness of wind, the depth of the sea, the steadiness of the earth, the firmness of rock.

I get up today with God's strength holding me up, God's power keeping me going, God's wisdom guiding me, God's eye watching ahead of me, God's ear listening for me, God's word speaking for me, God's hand guarding me, God's way opening in front of me.

Christ with me, Christ in front of me, Christ behind me, Christ inside me, Christ under me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Christ when I lie down, Christ when I sit down, Christ when I get up. Christ in the heart of every person who thinks of me, Christ in the mouth of everyone who speaks to me, Christ in every eye that sees me, Christ in every ear that hears me.

I get up today through a mighty strength — the strength of the Three in One, the Creator of creation.

About this prayer: known as the Lorica, or Breastplate, of St Patrick. The Irish text as we have it dates from around the eighth century; tradition ties it to Patrick himself in the fifth. A lorica is a prayer of encircling — you name Christ on every side until there is nowhere left uncovered. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Come, True Light"
author: "Symeon the New Theologian"
date: "c. 1010"
topics: [light, longing, presence, union with God]
excerpt: "A Byzantine monk names Christ eleven ways and still says it is not enough."
tags: [prayer]
---
Come, true light. Come, eternal life. Come, hidden secret. Come, treasure with no name. Come, thing no words reach. Come, person no mind holds.

Come, unending gladness. Come, light that never sets. Come, the hope of everyone who will be saved.

Come, you who raise the fallen. Come, you who wake the sleeping. Come — you who alone go to the one who is alone, because I am alone, as you can see.

Come, you who have become desire itself in me, who have made me want you, you who are entirely unapproachable. Come, my breath and my life. Come, the comfort of my poor soul. Come, my joy, my glory, my endless delight.

About this prayer: Symeon the New Theologian, abbot in eleventh-century Constantinople, is one of only three people the Eastern church has ever called "the Theologian". Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Day by Day"
author: "Richard of Chichester"
date: "c. 1253"
topics: [discipleship, love, gratitude, following]
excerpt: "Three requests, one sentence — the shortest complete prayer of discipleship in English."
tags: [prayer]
---
Thank you, Lord Jesus Christ, for all the good things you have given me — for all the pain and the insults you took for me.

Merciful friend, brother, redeemer: let me know you more clearly, love you more dearly, and follow you more nearly, day by day.

About this prayer: Richard of Chichester, a thirteenth-century English bishop, is said to have prayed it on his deathbed in 1253. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Eternal Trinity, You Are a Deep Sea.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Eternal Trinity, You Are a Deep Sea"
author: "Catherine of Siena"
date: "c. 1378"
topics: [the Trinity, longing, knowledge of God, hunger]
excerpt: "The more she is given, the hungrier she gets — Catherine's central image for knowing God."
tags: [prayer]
---
Eternal Trinity, you are a deep sea. The further I go into you, the more I find, and the more I find, the more I go looking for you.

You are never satisfied with what you give the soul. You never fill it so full that it stops being hungry — because in the depths of you, you feed the soul in a way that leaves it hungrier still.

Eternal Trinity, you are the fire that always burns and is never used up. You burn away everything false in me. You are the light that shows me the truth. In your light I have come to know your truth, and I have found you.

About this prayer: Catherine of Siena, a Dominican laywoman who could not write and dictated everything, ended her Dialogue with this. She had enough weight to tell a pope to go back to Rome, and he went. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Fire of Life"
author: "Hildegard of Bingen"
date: "c. 1150"
topics: [Holy Spirit, creation, life, healing]
excerpt: "Hildegard's Spirit is not a whisper but the vitality running through everything alive."
tags: [prayer]
---
Holy Spirit, you are the life in everything that lives. You move the whole creation and you are its root.

You wash everything clean, you scour away guilt, you soothe what is raw. You are the burning in real love and the sweetness in the heart, and your fragrance goes with what is good.

You are the clear spring, the one who gathers the scattered, the one who finds what is lost. You are the armour of the soul and the joining of everything that is joined. You are the water for the ones who are dry and the warmth for the ones who have gone cold.

Wake us. Set us on fire. Keep us alive.

About this prayer: Hildegard of Bingen — abbess, composer, physician, correspondent of emperors — described the Spirit in terms of green, growing vitality, a word she coined for it. She was named a Doctor of the Church in 2012, eight hundred years late. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Give Us a Pure Heart"
author: "Alcuin of York"
date: "c. 795"
topics: [purity, humility, faith, wisdom]
excerpt: "Six things asked for in one breath — the shortest complete rule of life in the collection."
tags: [prayer]
---
Give us, Lord, a clean heart, so that we may see you. Give us a humble heart, so that we may hear you. Give us a loving heart, so that we may serve you. Give us a believing heart, so that we may stay with you.

Give us a mind that knows the difference between what matters and what only feels urgent. And give us the courage to act on the difference.

About this prayer: Alcuin of York, the English scholar Charlemagne brought to his court to rebuild education across the Frankish empire. Much of what survived of classical learning survived because of the copying programme he ran. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Grant Me First to Ask Rightly.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Grant Me First to Ask Rightly"
author: "Benedict of Nursia"
date: "c. 530"
topics: [wisdom, discernment, beginnings, the Rule]
excerpt: "Benedict's prayer for the grace to want the right thing before asking for it."
tags: [prayer]
---
Gracious and holy Father, give me the intelligence to understand you, the perception to notice you, the patience to wait for you, and eyes that want to see you.

Give me a heart that thinks about you, a life that pleases you, and the persistence to keep on hoping in you. In the end, give me yourself — and let me have you with confidence.

Whatever good work you start in me, help me to ask for it properly, to seek it honestly, and to finish it completely, for the glory of your name.

About this prayer: Benedict of Nursia wrote the Rule that shaped Western monastic life for fifteen hundred years. His whole approach to prayer starts here — before asking God for anything, ask God to teach you what is worth asking for. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Grant Me, Lord, a Steady Heart.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Grant Me, Lord, a Steady Heart"
author: "Thomas Aquinas"
date: "c. 1270"
topics: [wisdom, steadiness, temptation, perseverance]
excerpt: "Aquinas asking for the kind of inner constancy that nothing can knock sideways."
tags: [prayer]
---
Give me, Lord my God, a mind that knows you, a determination that looks for you, a wisdom that finds you, and a life that pleases you.

Give me a steadiness that waits for you without giving up, and a confidence that finally takes hold of you.

Let me accept your discipline as correction, use what you give me along the way as help, and enjoy your happiness at the end as home.

About this prayer: Thomas Aquinas, the greatest systematic mind of the medieval church, prayed in far plainer language than he wrote in. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/I Do Not Know What to Ask For.md
notes.body:
---
title: "I Do Not Know What to Ask For"
author: "Philaret of Moscow"
date: "c. 1840"
topics: [surrender, guidance, unanswered prayer, trust]
excerpt: "The prayer for the moment when you genuinely cannot tell what to ask God for."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I do not know what to ask you for. You alone know what I need. You love me better than I know how to love myself.

Father, give your child what he does not know to ask for. I do not dare ask for a cross or for comfort — I can only wait here. My heart is open to you.

Come to me and help me, for the sake of your great mercy. Strike me and heal me, knock me down and lift me up. I am quiet, and I say nothing back. I have no wish except to do what you want. Teach me to pray. And pray in me yourself.

About this prayer: Philaret, Metropolitan of Moscow through much of the nineteenth century, oversaw the first translation of the Bible into modern Russian. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "In the Hands of God"
author: "Teresa of Ávila"
date: "c. 1570"
topics: [surrender, guidance, trust, vocation]
excerpt: "Teresa handing over the steering — a prayer for anyone who cannot see the next step."
tags: [prayer]
---
I am yours; you made me. I am yours; you called me. I am yours; you waited for me. I am yours; I did not get away from you.

So what do you want from me? Give me riches or poverty, comfort or hardship, light or dark, whatever you like. Send me where you want and use me as you please.

I want nothing except to be what you want me to be.

About this prayer: Teresa of Ávila, who spent twenty years in prayer she described as mostly dry before anything changed. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Keep Watch, Dear Lord"
author: "Benedictine Compline"
date: "c. 800"
topics: [night, sleep, suffering, rest, the dying]
excerpt: "The last prayer of the monastic day — said in the dark, on behalf of everyone who is awake in it."
tags: [prayer]
---
Keep watch, Lord, with everyone who is working or awake or crying tonight, and give your angels charge over those who are asleep.

Look after the sick, Lord Christ. Give rest to the ones who are worn out. Bless the ones who are dying. Comfort the ones who are suffering. Have pity on the ones in distress. Protect the ones who are happy.

And all of it for the sake of your love. Amen.

About this prayer: from Compline, the last of the monastic hours, prayed just before the night silence. Monks said it standing in the dark, deliberately naming the people who would not be sleeping. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Let Me Know What Is Worth Knowing.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Let Me Know What Is Worth Knowing"
author: "Thomas à Kempis"
date: "c. 1420"
topics: [humility, wisdom, discernment, self-knowledge]
excerpt: "From The Imitation of Christ — a prayer against learning that makes you worse."
tags: [prayer]
---
Give me, Lord, the sense to know what is actually worth knowing, to value what is actually worth valuing, and above all to look for whatever pleases you most.

Do not let me judge things by how they look or hear about them by what people say. Let me tell the difference between what is spiritual and what is not, and above all keep me searching for what you want.

Often our senses mislead us in judging things. And often people who trust their own eyes get it wrong too.

About this prayer: Thomas à Kempis, a Dutch monk, wrote The Imitation of Christ around 1420. After the Bible it is probably the most widely read Christian book ever written. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Let Nothing Trouble You"
author: "Teresa of Ávila"
date: "c. 1570"
topics: [anxiety, patience, trust, contentment]
excerpt: "The lines Teresa kept in her breviary — nine short sentences against fear."
tags: [prayer]
---
Let nothing trouble you. Let nothing frighten you.

Everything passes. God does not change.

Patience gets you everything. Whoever has God is short of nothing.

God alone is enough.

About this prayer: Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite reformer, wrote it in her own hand on a bookmark kept in her prayer book, found after her death in 1582. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Lord of All Pots and Pans.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Lord of All Pots and Pans"
author: "Brother Lawrence"
date: "c. 1680"
topics: [ordinary life, work, presence of God, faithfulness]
excerpt: "A monastery cook's prayer over the washing-up — God in the kitchen, not only the chapel."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord of all pots and pans and things — since I have no time to be a saint by doing lovely things, or watching late with you, or dreaming in the light, or storming heaven's gates — make me a saint by getting meals and washing up the plates.

Lord, I cannot do this work unless you are in it with me. I am not asking for the feeling of your presence. I am asking to keep doing the next thing in front of me as if it were done for you, because it is.

About this prayer: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection spent thirty years in the kitchen of a Carmelite monastery in Paris and taught that he was as close to God among the pots as he was at the altar. His conversations were collected after his death as The Practice of the Presence of God. The verse form here is a later English rendering in his spirit.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Lord, Grant Me the Living Fountain.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Lord, Grant Me the Living Fountain"
author: "Columbanus"
date: "c. 600"
topics: [thirst, longing, the word, satisfaction]
excerpt: "An Irish monk in Italy, asking for a thirst that does not go away."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, give me the fountain that never dries up — the one whose water tastes so good that it makes people want more of it, not less.

Sweet and clear stream, running down from the hills: let my inner self drink from you. Let me be soaked in you, and let your streams run through me — not just a drop, but enough to soak the ground.

I do not want the kind of drink that ends thirst. I want the kind that makes me thirstier. Let me always be looking for you, and always finding you, and always looking again.

About this prayer: Columbanus, the Irish monk who founded monasteries across France and Italy and died at Bobbio in 615. He was one of the most influential missionaries of the early medieval West. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Most High, Glorious God"
author: "Francis of Assisi"
date: "c. 1206"
topics: [surrender, faith, beginnings, obedience]
excerpt: "The prayer the young Francis said in front of a broken crucifix, before he knew what he was for."
tags: [prayer]
---
Most high, glorious God, light up the dark of my heart.

Give me faith that holds, hope that is real, and love that is complete. Give me the sense and the awareness, Lord, to do what you actually, truly want me to do.

About this prayer: Francis of Assisi prayed it in the ruined chapel of San Damiano around 1206, before he had given away his inheritance and before there was any such thing as a Franciscan. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Pierce My Soul"
author: "Bonaventure"
date: "c. 1260"
topics: [love, the cross, desire, surrender]
excerpt: "A Franciscan asks to be wounded by love rather than merely persuaded by it."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord Jesus, pierce the deepest part of me with the sweet and healthy wound of your love — with real, calm, holy, apostolic love. Let my soul always be faint with loving you and longing for you.

Let it want you and lose itself in your courtyards. Let it long to be free of the body and be with you. Let it go hungry for you, the bread of angels, the food of holy souls, our daily bread.

Let my heart always be hungry for you and feeding on you. Let the deepest part of me be filled with the sweetness of having you.

About this prayer: Bonaventure, minister general of the Franciscans and a professor at Paris alongside Aquinas, wrote it in The Soul's Journey into God. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Prayer for Generosity"
author: "Ignatius of Loyola"
date: "c. 1540"
topics: [service, generosity, cost, obedience]
excerpt: "A soldier's prayer, from a soldier who became a monk — serve without keeping score."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, teach me to be generous. Teach me to serve you the way you deserve — to give without counting the cost, to fight without worrying about the wounds, to work without looking for rest, to spend myself without asking for anything back, except knowing that I am doing what you want.

About this prayer: long attributed to Ignatius of Loyola, who was a soldier before a wound at Pamplona put him in a bed with nothing to read but the lives of the saints. The military language is his own. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Monastic/Prayer of a Soul Taken with Love.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Prayer of a Soul Taken with Love"
author: "John of the Cross"
date: "c. 1580"
topics: [love, desire, boldness, inheritance]
excerpt: "The boldest claim in monastic prayer: everything God has made is already mine."
tags: [prayer]
---
Mine are the heavens and mine is the earth. Mine are the nations, the good people are mine and the sinners are mine. The angels are mine, and the mother of God, and everything is mine. God himself is mine and for me — because Christ is mine and all for me.

So what are you asking for, my soul? All of it is yours, and all of it is for you. Do not settle for less, and do not stop at the crumbs that fall from your Father's table.

Go out and be glad in your glory. Hide yourself in it and enjoy it, and you will get everything your heart asks for.

About this prayer: John of the Cross, Spanish Carmelite and poet, wrote it while or shortly after being imprisoned by his own order in a cell too small to stand up in. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Take, Lord, and Receive"
author: "Ignatius of Loyola"
date: "c. 1535"
topics: [surrender, freedom, grace, offering]
excerpt: "The Suscipe — the last and hardest prayer of the Spiritual Exercises."
tags: [prayer]
---
Take, Lord, and receive all my freedom, my memory, my understanding, and everything I decide — everything I have and everything I own.

You gave it all to me. I hand it all back to you, Lord. It is yours now; do with it exactly what you want.

Give me only your love and your grace. That is enough for me. I am not asking for anything else.

About this prayer: Ignatius of Loyola places it at the very end of the Spiritual Exercises, after weeks of preparation, because it is not a prayer you can mean on the first day. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Teach Me to Seek You"
author: "Anselm of Canterbury"
date: "c. 1078"
topics: [seeking God, faith, understanding, desire]
excerpt: "Anselm's prayer at the opening of the Proslogion — faith looking for understanding."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, teach me to look for you, and show yourself to me when I look — because I cannot look for you unless you teach me how, and I will never find you unless you show yourself.

Let me look for you by wanting you, and want you by looking for you. Let me find you by loving you, and love you by finding you.

I am not trying to reach the top of your greatness, because my understanding is nowhere near it. But I do want to understand a little of the truth my heart already believes and loves. I do not try to understand so that I can believe — I believe so that I can understand.

About this prayer: Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote it around 1078 at the start of the Proslogion. The last sentence became one of the most quoted lines in Christian thought. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "The Canticle of the Creatures"
author: "Francis of Assisi"
date: "1225"
topics: [creation, praise, death, gratitude]
excerpt: "Francis, nearly blind and close to death, calls the sun and moon his brother and sister."
tags: [prayer]
---
Most high, all-powerful, good Lord — the praise, the glory, the honour and every blessing belong to you. To you alone, Most High, and no one is fit even to say your name.

Praise you, my Lord, with everything you have made, and first of all Brother Sun, who brings the day and the light you give us through him. He is beautiful and he shines out brilliantly, and he carries something of you, Most High.

Praise you, my Lord, for Sister Moon and the stars — you made them in the sky, clear and precious and lovely. Praise you for Brother Wind, and for air and clouds and every kind of weather, by which you keep alive everything you have made. Praise you for Sister Water, so useful and humble and precious and clean. Praise you for Brother Fire, who lights up the night, and is beautiful and cheerful and strong.

Praise you, my Lord, for our sister, Mother Earth, who holds us up and looks after us, and produces all kinds of fruit, and coloured flowers, and grass.

Praise you, my Lord, for the people who forgive because they love you, and who put up with illness and trouble. The ones who bear it peacefully are blessed, because you, Most High, will crown them.

Praise you, my Lord, for our Sister Bodily Death, whom no living person escapes. Blessed are the ones she finds doing what you want.

Praise and bless my Lord, and thank him, and serve him with great humility.

About this prayer: Francis composed it in 1225, a year before his death, when he was nearly blind and in constant pain. The last verse, on death, he added when he was told he had only weeks left. It is the earliest surviving poem in the Italian language. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "The Jesus Prayer"
author: "Desert tradition"
date: "c. 500"
topics: [mercy, repentance, constant prayer, simplicity]
excerpt: "Eight words the church has repeated for fifteen hundred years, matched to the breath."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.

Say it once. Say it a hundred times. Say it walking, say it in a queue, say it when you cannot think of anything else to say. Let it go in with the breath and out with the breath until it says itself.

It is not a formula, and repeating it is not the point — Jesus is the point. But it is short enough to survive a bad day, and honest enough to survive a good one.

About this prayer: it grew out of the fourth-century desert fathers and became the heart of Eastern Christian practice, taught in the collection called the Philokalia. It joins the blind man's cry in Luke 18 to the tax collector's prayer in the same chapter.

---
title: "The Optina Elders' Morning Prayer"
author: "The Elders of Optina"
date: "c. 1850"
topics: [morning, surrender, peace, acceptance]
excerpt: "The Russian monastic prayer for taking the day as it comes rather than as you planned it."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, let me meet everything this day brings with peace in me. Let me give myself completely to what you want.

At every hour of this day, show me what to do and how to do it. Whatever news reaches me, teach me to take it with a settled mind and the firm conviction that your will is behind all of it.

In everything I say and do, guide my thoughts and feelings. When things I did not expect happen, do not let me forget that they came from you.

Teach me to deal honestly and sensibly with everyone, and not to upset or embarrass anyone. Give me the strength to get through this day and everything in it. Guide what I want. Teach me to pray. And pray in me yourself.

About this prayer: from Optina Monastery, the Russian house that drew Gogol, Dostoevsky and Tolstoy to its elders in the nineteenth century. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Before Reading Scripture"
author: "John Calvin"
date: "c. 1550"
topics: [scripture, illumination, teachability, obedience]
excerpt: "Calvin's prayer for the Spirit's light before opening the Bible."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, we are opening your word, and we know that we cannot understand it by ourselves.

Give us the light of your Spirit, so that what we read here does not stay information but becomes life. Give us teachable hearts — willing to be corrected, not only informed.

And let us not stop at understanding it. Let us do it.

About this prayer: John Calvin ended almost every lecture with a short prayer, and opened his study of Scripture the same way. He was firm that the Spirit who inspired the text is the same Spirit needed to read it. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Collect for Purity"
author: "Thomas Cranmer"
date: "1549"
topics: [holiness, worship, honesty, the heart]
excerpt: "The prayer that opens Anglican worship — nothing hidden, nothing pretended."
tags: [prayer]
---
Almighty God, every heart is open to you, everything we want is known to you, and no secret is hidden from you.

Clean out the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of your Holy Spirit, so that we may love you completely and properly praise your holy name. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

About this prayer: Thomas Cranmer translated it from a much older Latin collect into the first English Prayer Book of 1549. Anglican worship has begun with it for nearly five hundred years — it is deliberately placed first, before anything else is said. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Communion with God"
author: "John Owen"
date: "c. 1657"
topics: [the Trinity, assurance, fellowship, grace]
excerpt: "Owen on knowing all three Persons distinctly — not God in general."
tags: [prayer]
---
Father, let me not settle for knowing about you when you have opened the way to know you.

Let me have real dealings with all three of you: with the Father in his love, which is where everything started and where nothing is owed; with the Son in his grace, who bought what I could never afford; with the Spirit in his comfort, who takes what is true and makes it true to me.

Keep me from a general religiousness that has a word for God and no acquaintance with him. And when I cannot feel any of it, hold me to what is true anyway.

About this prayer: John Owen, vice-chancellor of Oxford under Cromwell and the most formidable of the Puritan theologians, wrote Of Communion with God. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Evening Confession"
author: "Lancelot Andrewes"
date: "c. 1610"
topics: [confession, evening, mercy, honesty]
excerpt: "A bishop's private confession at the end of the day — specific, unsparing, and hopeful."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I have left undone the things I should have done, and I have done the things I should not have done. There is no health in me, but you are a God of health.

I have sinned in what I thought, in what I said, in what I did, and in what I let happen. I have wasted the day you gave me.

But you are merciful, and you save. You take no pleasure in the death of a sinner. Turn me, and I will be turned. Take me back tonight, and let me start again tomorrow.

About this prayer: Lancelot Andrewes, bishop of Winchester and one of the chief translators of the King James Bible, kept a book of private devotions in Greek, Hebrew and Latin, never meant for publication. It was found after his death in 1626. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Evening Prayer"
author: "Jeremy Taylor"
date: "c. 1650"
topics: [evening, examination, mercy, rest]
excerpt: "The examined day, handed over before sleep."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, another day is gone, and I am one day nearer home.

Let me look at it honestly before I sleep. Show me what I did today that I would not want you to have seen. Show me the good I could have done and did not, because it was inconvenient. Do not let me talk myself out of either.

Forgive what is past. I cannot fetch this day back and do it again. Take it, mend what can be mended, and let me lie down at peace — not because the day was good, but because you are.

About this prayer: Jeremy Taylor, chaplain to Charles I and later bishop, wrote Holy Living and Holy Dying during the English Civil War. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "For the Church"
author: "Philipp Melanchthon"
date: "c. 1540"
topics: [the church, unity, truth, peace]
excerpt: "Luther's quieter colleague, praying for a church tearing itself apart."
tags: [prayer]
---
Almighty God, look on your church. She is torn, and much of the tearing is our own doing.

Gather the scattered. Restrain the ones who love the argument more than the truth — and start with me if I am one of them. Give us teachers who are honest, pastors who are patient, and people willing to be taught.

Keep for us the pure teaching of your gospel, and keep us from mistaking our own sharpness for your truth. Give peace to your church, and let it be a peace built on what is true, not on everyone agreeing to say less.

About this prayer: Philipp Melanchthon wrote the Augsburg Confession and spent his life trying to hold together what Luther's boldness had broken open. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "General Thanksgiving"
author: "Book of Common Prayer"
date: "1662"
topics: [thanksgiving, gratitude, grace, daily prayer]
excerpt: "The Prayer Book's great thank-you — for creation, for rescue, and for the hope of more."
tags: [prayer]
---
Almighty God, Father of all mercies, we your unworthy servants thank you, with everything in us, for all your goodness and kindness to us and to everyone.

We bless you for making us and keeping us going, and for everything good in this life. But above all we bless you for your immeasurable love in redeeming the world through our Lord Jesus Christ — for the means of grace, and for the hope of glory.

Give us the sense of what all this is worth, so that our hearts are honestly grateful, and so that we show it not just with our mouths but with our lives — by handing ourselves over to your service and walking in holiness and uprightness all our days. Amen.

About this prayer: written by Edward Reynolds for the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. The phrase "the means of grace, and the hope of glory" has passed into ordinary English. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Give Me a Praying Heart"
author: "John Bunyan"
date: "c. 1662"
topics: [prayer, sincerity, the heart, weakness]
excerpt: "Bunyan on the difference between saying prayers and praying."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I would rather have a heart without words than words without a heart.

You have never yet turned away a broken prayer from a broken heart. When I cannot find the words, take the groan. When I cannot find the feeling, take the will. When I cannot even find the will, take the wanting to want it.

Teach me that prayer is not a performance you are grading, but a child pulling at his father's sleeve.

About this prayer: John Bunyan, the tinker from Bedford who wrote The Pilgrim's Progress, spent twelve years in prison for preaching without a licence. His short book on prayer insists that God hears the heart, not the vocabulary. Rendered here in modern English.

notes.path: Prayers/Reformers/Glory to You, My God, This Night.md
notes.body:
---
title: "Glory to You, My God, This Night"
author: "Thomas Ken"
date: "1674"
topics: [night, sleep, protection, thanksgiving]
excerpt: "The evening hymn whose last verse became the Doxology sung in half the churches in the world."
tags: [prayer]
---
Glory to you, my God, tonight, for all the blessings of the light. Keep me, keep me, King of kings, under the shadow of your wings.

Forgive me, Lord, for your dear Son, the wrong that I today have done — so that I may rest at peace with you, with everyone, and with myself.

Teach me to live, so that I may not be afraid to lie in my grave. Teach me to die, so that I may rise up glorious at the last day.

Praise God, from whom all blessings flow. Praise him, all creatures here below. Praise him above, you heavenly host. Praise Father, Son and Holy Ghost.

About this prayer: Thomas Ken, bishop of Bath and Wells, wrote it for the boys of Winchester College to sing in their rooms. The last verse is now simply "the Doxology". Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Light Such a Candle"
author: "Hugh Latimer"
date: "1555"
topics: [courage, martyrdom, faithfulness, hope]
excerpt: "Latimer's word to the man tied to the same stake — and the prayer behind it."
tags: [prayer]
---
Be of good comfort. Play the man. We shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.

Lord, I am an old man and afraid, and I would rather this cup went past me. Take the fear and leave the faithfulness. If our deaths are what you use, then use them — only do not let this be for nothing.

About this prayer: Hugh Latimer, former bishop of Worcester, said the first line to Nicholas Ridley as the fire was lit at Oxford in October 1555. Both were burned under Mary I. The second paragraph is a rendering of the fear his sermons freely admitted. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Lord, Make Me Willing"
author: "Richard Baxter"
date: "c. 1660"
topics: [surrender, obedience, contentment, self-denial]
excerpt: "The Puritan pastor's covenant prayer — no conditions attached."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, I am not my own. I am yours. Put me where you want me. Put me with whoever you want. Give me work or give me nothing to do. Let me be used or let me be set aside. Lift me up or bring me low. Let me have everything or let me have nothing.

I hand over everything I have and everything I am, freely and wholeheartedly, to what you decide.

And now, glorious and blessed God — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — you are mine and I am yours. Let it be so.

About this prayer: Richard Baxter pastored at Kidderminster and wrote The Reformed Pastor. This covenant form was later reworked by John Wesley into the Methodist Covenant Prayer still used on New Year's Eve. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Luther's Morning Prayer"
author: "Martin Luther"
date: "1529"
topics: [morning, protection, family, daily prayer]
excerpt: "The prayer Luther put in the Small Catechism for ordinary households to say at the start of the day."
tags: [prayer]
---
I thank you, my heavenly Father, through Jesus Christ your dear Son, that you kept me safe through the night from all harm and danger.

I ask you to keep me today too from sin and from everything that would hurt me, so that everything I do and how I live pleases you.

I put myself into your hands — my body, my soul, everything. Let your holy angel be with me, so that the evil one gets no hold on me. Amen.

About this prayer: Martin Luther wrote it into the Small Catechism of 1529, for parents to teach their children. He told them to say it, then get on with their work cheerfully and, if they liked, sing while they did. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Open the King's Eyes"
author: "William Tyndale"
date: "1536"
topics: [scripture, martyrdom, translation, courage]
excerpt: "The last words of the man who put the English Bible into English, spoken at the stake."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, open the King of England's eyes.

You gave your word to be heard, not locked up. You put it in the mouths of fishermen and tax collectors, in the language people argued and traded and grieved in. Do not let it be kept from the ploughboy because it is inconvenient to the palace.

I have not lived long enough to finish. Finish it without me.

About this prayer: William Tyndale was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde in 1536 for translating the Bible into English. His last words are recorded as the first line here. Within four years an English Bible drawing heavily on his work was in every parish church by royal command; roughly eighty per cent of the King James New Testament is his wording. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "Thanksgiving After Being Robbed"
author: "Matthew Henry"
date: "c. 1700"
topics: [gratitude, loss, perspective, providence]
excerpt: "The commentator's diary entry after being mugged — four reasons to be thankful."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord, let me thank you first that I was never robbed before. Second, that although they took my wallet, they did not take my life. Third, that although they took everything I had, it was not much. And fourth, that it was me who was robbed and not me who did the robbing.

Teach me to count like this more often — not to pretend the loss is nothing, but to notice how much is still here.

About this prayer: Matthew Henry, whose commentary on the whole Bible is still in print three hundred years later, wrote this in his diary the evening he was robbed. Rendered here in modern English.

---
title: "You Are My Righteousness"
author: "Martin Luther"
date: "c. 1520"
topics: [justification, assurance, grace, exchange]
excerpt: "Luther's shortest summary of the gospel, addressed straight to Christ."
tags: [prayer]
---
Lord Jesus, you are my righteousness, and I am your sin. You took on what was mine, and you gave me what was yours. You became what you were not, so that I could become what I was not.

Give me the sense to stop looking at myself for evidence, and to look at you instead. When my conscience accuses me, let me not argue with it — let me point it to you.

About this prayer: drawn from Luther's letters and his commentary on Galatians, where the "joyful exchange" is his central image for justification. Rendered here in modern English.
